title: The divine dance
hook: Greek fathers described the three persons as dwelling in one another, like a round dance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the filioque: one Latin word, and the Son, added to a creed in the West and not in the East. Your line was one word, long argument. Did you say the creed both ways? Day one thousand seventy-two.

A circle of people at a wedding, arms on each other's shoulders, stepping to the left, then the right. Nobody in the circle is the center. Nobody leads for long. If one person stops, the whole ring feels it. And if you ask where the dance is, you can't point to any one dancer. It's in all of them, and between them, at the same time. Some Christian writers have reached for exactly that picture to talk about God. Not a ruler on a throne this time, and not a triangle on a whiteboard. A ring of movement. Two days ago, every picture of the Trinity fell short. This one falls short too, but it falls short in a lively way. Today's word is the Greek name for it.

Perichoresis. Greek Christian writers used it for something Jesus says in John's Gospel. In the King James Bible, he asks Philip: "Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" Not beside. In. The Father in the Son, the Son in the Father. Later in the same Gospel, praying for his friends, he widens it: "as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Teachers in the Greek-speaking churches, John of Damascus among them, used perichoresis to name that mutual in-ness: Father, Son and Spirit each dwelling in the others, without blurring into one another and without being split apart. Each makes room for the others. Each is at home in the others. Now the dance. In English the word sounds like choreography, and some modern writers have run with that: God as a round dance, three persons moving in one movement. Other readers point out that the word's root is about going around and making room, not dancing, and they'd rather keep the picture loose. Both agree on what the picture is for. It says God is not a lonely thing. Before there was anything, Christians say, there was already giving and receiving, love going out and coming back. And then the prayer in John: that they also may be one in us. The circle has a gap in it, and the gap is held open. Christians differ on how far to push that. Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life. Others put it more carefully. Either way, the ring in this picture is not closed.
screen: `I IN THE FATHER, THE FATHER IN ME.`
`A RING WITH A GAP HELD OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move in a circle, slowly. If you can stand, stand. Turn, very slowly, all the way round, taking a full breath for each step. Notice the room passing: a wall, a window, a door, back to where you began. If standing isn't possible, trace a slow circle with one hand instead. As you turn, think of the people who make room for you, and the people you make room for. If you pray, you can say the line from John: that they also may be one in us. If you don't, just keep turning, and let the circle be the whole of it. The bell holds the time.
Perichoresis. The persons of the Trinity dwelling in one another, each making room for the others: some say, like a dance.
Your line: god is a dance. Today, in one conversation, make room: step back so someone else can step in. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant theologians use the word perichoresis when they teach about the Trinity, and some churches have icons and hymns that speak of the three persons dwelling in one another.

notes: The index hook says 'like a round dance'. Perichoresis is usually derived from perichoreo (to go around, to make room), not choreuo (to dance); the dance picture is a popular modern association. The script presents both views without stating an etymology as fact. Confirm wording.
John of Damascus named as one Greek teacher who used perichoresis of the Trinity (Exposition 1.8, 1.14); confirm the chapter references.
'Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life' points toward theosis; confirm it is fair, and that 'others put it more carefully' does not rank anyone.
'Last week's pictures of the Trinity' refers to day 1070 (Pictures of the Trinity), which falls in the previous week (days 1065–1071). Confirm.
Practice invites a slow turn in a circle, with a hand-tracing alternative for anyone who can't stand.
